desc:
A grid matrix contains only 0 and 1. You may rearrange its columns in any order you like (each column moves as a whole; rows are not changed). After that, look for the largest rectangle of cells that are all 1.

Return the largest area (number of cells) such a rectangle can have, over all possible column orders. Equivalently: choose a block of consecutive rows and a set of columns that are all 1 in every row of the block, and maximise rows times columns.

Example: [[0,0,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]] gives 4: put the two columns that are 1 in the last two rows side by side to get a 2 by 2 block of ones.
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: If the column order were fixed this would be the maximal rectangle of ones. Since you can reorder columns, which property of a column matters for a given bottom row?
Fix the bottom row of the rectangle. Column c contributes a stack of consecutive ones of some height h[c] ending at that row, and only those heights matter.
For a fixed bottom row, sort the heights in descending order. Taking the first k columns gives a rectangle of area k * (k-th largest height); maximise over k and over all bottom rows.
editorial: For every row r maintain h[c]: the number of consecutive ones in column c ending at row r (0 if the cell is 0). A rectangle whose bottom edge is on row r and which uses a set S of columns can have height min(h[c] for c in S). Because the columns can be arranged freely, the set S does not need to be contiguous in the original grid.

To use k columns the best choice is the k columns with the largest heights, giving area k * (k-th largest of h). Sort h in descending order and evaluate every k. Doing this for each row costs O(C log C), so the whole algorithm is O(R * C log C) time and O(C) space; counting sort can bring it to O(R * C).
